target.title: fix: backup skips volatile cache paths
target.body:
Closes #98865

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `openclaw backup create` could archive disposable agent runtime cache, browser cache, retired archive, and transient side-effect files from runtime-owned state paths. Those paths can be large or short-lived during live operation, so including them can bloat backups or make archive creation fail if a disposable file disappears while tar is walking the tree.

## Why This Change Was Made

The backup volatile-path filter now covers agent runtime tmp/cache/shell snapshot directories, managed browser user-data cache/resource directories, retired archive paths, and non-SQLite transient lock/partial/WAL/SHM/journal paths under transient-owned roots while preserving durable agent auth/profile files, browser profile files, and installed plugin source under `state/extensions`. The archive writer also gives node-tar a backup-scoped synthetic stat cache for known volatile paths so entries that vanish before `lstat` still reach the normal filtered skip path; SQLite sidecars remain under the existing SQLite snapshot safety checks instead of the generic volatile path.

## User Impact

Backup archives are smaller and more reliable during live OpenClaw use. Operators still get durable state such as agent auth profiles, browser profile preferences/cookies, and installed plugin source lockfiles, while disposable runtime/cache paths are counted in `skippedVolatileCount` and omitted from the tarball.

## Evidence

- Source/dependency check: `tar@7.5.16` calls `filter` only after `lstat` succeeds in `Pack`, so a disappeared file can reject before the existing filter sees it; the new scoped `statCache` handles only paths already classified as volatile.
- Real backup behavior after repair: with an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` containing agent cache, browser `Default/Cache`, a retired archive path, transient-root `cache/queue/item.wal` and `downloads/download.partial`, durable browser `Default/Preferences`, and durable `state/extensions/example/{Cargo.lock,download.partial}`, running `pnpm openclaw backup create --output <tmp>/out --no-include-workspace --json` produced `skippedVolatileCount=5`; `tar -tzf` showed durable browser preferences and both `state/extensions` files, and did not show the cache/archive/transient-root side-effect paths.
- Real agent turn: `pnpm openclaw agent --local --agent proof --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro --message "Reply with exactly: backup proof agent ok" --json --timeout 180` completed through provider `deepseek`, model `deepseek-v4-pro`, HTTP status 200, final text `backup proof agent ok`.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/backup-volatile-filter.test.ts src/infra/backup-create.test.ts` passed after repair: 63 unit-fast tests and 39 infra tests.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo && node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo` passed after repair.
- `pnpm format:fix -- src/infra/backup-volatile-filter.ts src/infra/backup-volatile-filter.test.ts src/infra/backup-create.test.ts` passed after repair.
- `pnpm format:docs:check -- docs/cli/backup.md` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed after repair.
- `pnpm build` passed after repair.
- `./.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode local` passed after repair with no accepted/actionable findings.

target.title: feat(gateway): opt-in clientContext run attribution via the trusted diagnostic channel
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Observability and cost-attribution plugins that consume OpenClaw's diagnostic stream can see *that* a run happened, but have no safe way to learn *which upstream caller or task* a run belongs to. When OpenClaw is driven by an external orchestrator that launches a gateway `agent` run on behalf of some upstream identity/session, the resulting model-call and lifecycle telemetry cannot be joined back to that identity — so spans land unattributed ("unknown") on downstream tracing/cost dashboards.

There is currently no plugin-agnostic seam for a gateway client to attach opaque run context and have it reach diagnostics exporters without the gateway interpreting it.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an optional, bounded, opaque `clientContext` bag that a gateway `agent` request can carry, and deliver it to exporters over the **existing trusted diagnostic grant** (`onTrustedInternalDiagnosticEvent`, exposed to plugins via `ctx.internalDiagnostics.onEvent`) — not on the public event payload. No new subscription API is introduced.

Design decisions and boundaries:

- **Trusted-grant-only delivery.** `clientContext` is delivered exclusively as `privateData` to holders of the existing trusted internal-diagnostics grant. Public `message.queued` / `session.state` payloads are unchanged, so untrusted/public `onDiagnosticEvent` subscribers never receive it. Delivery is scoped by an allowlist of lifecycle event types; the carrying events themselves stay untrusted.
- **Core stays opaque.** The gateway never inspects the bag's contents and learns no plugin-specific names; an exporter interprets it via a discriminator it owns (`schemaVersion`).
- **Bounded and sanitized.** `diagnostic-client-context.ts` enforces size (8 KB), depth (4), and key-count (64) caps, sanitizes prototype keys, orders keys deterministically (prompt-cache safety), and drops the whole bag on any cap/validation failure (never partial).
- **Run-scoped attribution.** Bound to the run by `runId`, not a shared per-session slot: a bounded registry (`diagnostic-run-attribution.ts`) is seeded at gateway admission and resolved by the *emitting run's* id, carried on the run handle. Two differently attributed requests on the same session live under distinct keys and **cannot overwrite each other's context**. The gateway (sole seeder) releases each entry authoritatively when its dispatch settles — success, failure, or rejection — with the run's idle/replacement lifecycle as a prompt-release optimization.
- **Inert when absent or disabled.** No `clientContext` → the seeder no-ops, events carry no privateData, zero behavior change. Diagnostics disabled → nothing is captured.

## User Impact

Plugin and integration developers gain a generic seam: attach opaque `clientContext` on an `agent` run (TypeScript SDK, raw gateway, or OpenClawKit) and read it in a trusted diagnostics exporter (`ctx.internalDiagnostics.onEvent`) to attribute spans/cost to the upstream identity. Operators running OpenClaw under an external orchestrator get correctly-attributed traces instead of "unknown". No impact on existing runs or on public diagnostic consumers.

## Compatibility

All changed public surfaces are additive. Accounting for each:

| Surface | Change | Compatibility |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway `agent` request (`packages/gateway-protocol`) | `+ clientContext?` (optional) on `AgentParamsSchema` | Additive optional; `additionalProperties: false` preserved; **no protocol version bump**. Absent → unchanged. |
| Public diagnostic events (`message.queued` / `session.state`) | **none** | Payloads unchanged. `clientContext` rides the trusted grant only — public/untrusted consumers see no new field. |
| `DiagnosticEventPrivateData` (trusted-grant payload) | `+ clientContext?` | Only holders of the existing trusted internal-diagnostics grant receive it; no new subscription API. |
| TypeScript SDK (`packages/sdk`) | `+ clientContext?` on run creation | Additive optional; existing callers unaffected. |
| Swift `GatewayModels.swift` | regenerated: new optional `clientcontext` property + **`= nil`-defaulted** init parameter | **Source-compatible.** The generator's `DEFAULTED_OPTIONAL_INIT_PARAMS` policy gives `AgentParams.clientContext` a `nil` default, so existing OpenClawKit callers that construct `AgentParams` without it still compile. |
| Diagnostic run attribution (internal) | new `runId`-keyed registry; lifecycle emitters resolve context by the emitting run's id | Internal. Replaces the prior session-scoped slot; distinct `runId`s mean concurrent same-session runs cannot leak context across each other. |

No `CHANGELOG.md` edit (left for maintainers per CONTRIBUTING).

## Security / telemetry boundary

`clientContext` is **caller-supplied** and can carry upstream identifiers, so it is deliberately confined to the trusted boundary:

- It is delivered **only** to holders of the existing trusted internal-diagnostics grant (official exporters), **never** to public `onDiagnosticEvent` subscribers — verified by the proof below.
- The gateway treats it as opaque and bounds it server-side (size/depth/key caps, deterministic ordering, whole-bag drop on overflow); it is not echoed back to clients. It is only retained when diagnostics are enabled.
- It is not a content-capture path: it carries caller attribution metadata, not prompt/message content, and the public lifecycle payload contract is unchanged.

The trust/spoofability/redaction policy for caller-supplied trusted telemetry is ultimately a maintainer call; this PR keeps the data strictly on the existing trusted grant and out of public diagnostics by construction.

## Evidence

**Focused tests (local, this branch):**

- `src/infra/diagnostic-client-context.test.ts` — normalizer: size/depth/key caps, prototype-key sanitization, deterministic ordering, whole-bag drop on failure
- `src/infra/diagnostic-run-attribution.test.ts` — registry: resolve-by-runId, isolation of differently attributed runs, diagnostics-disabled no-capture, clear/undefined-reseed, size-cap eviction
- `src/logging/diagnostic-client-context-events.test.ts` — seed → trusted-grant inheritance; public listeners excluded; **two differently attributed same-session runs stay isolated**; clear-on-idle bounding; absent → no privateData
- `src/infra/diagnostic-events.test.ts` — dispatch/emitter regression incl. trusted-vs-public delivery
- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/agent.test.ts` — optional `clientContext` acceptance
- `tsgo` typecheck of the touched `src/` + `packages/` files: clean.

CI runs the full suite.

### Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** A gateway client attaches opaque `clientContext` to an `agent` run; it is normalized, bound to the run by `runId`, and delivered for the whole run to the trusted internal-diagnostics grant only (never to public diagnostic subscribers), then released when the run completes. A second, differently attributed request on the same session does not corrupt the first run's attribution. Absent or oversized context is a no-op.

**Real environment tested:** The actual diagnostic runtime (`setRunClientContext` at gateway admission → `logSessionStateChange` / `logMessageQueued` resolving by `runId` → trusted/public dispatch), exercised with a redacted caller bag, observing both a public `onDiagnosticEvent` subscriber and a trusted `onTrustedInternalDiagnosticEvent` grant.

**Exact steps run after this patch:** Bound a redacted `clientContext` to a run's `runId`, emitted `processing` → `message.queued` → `idle (run_completed)` → a trailing `message.queued`, and captured what each channel observed:

```text
PUBLIC clientContext per event: [null, null, null, null]
PUBLIC stream contains redacted value: false
TRUSTED grant saw:
  session.state   clientContext = { schemaVersion: "agentweave.context.v1", upstreamRunId: "REDACTED-run-7f3a2c" }   # processing
  message.queued  clientContext = { schemaVersion: "agentweave.context.v1", upstreamRunId: "REDACTED-run-7f3a2c" }   # queued
  session.state   clientContext = { schemaVersion: "agentweave.context.v1", upstreamRunId: "REDACTED-run-7f3a2c" }   # idle (completing run)
  message.queued  (no clientContext)                                                                                 # trailing event after the run cleared
```

**Run-isolation proof (the same-session race):** two runs `run-A` (UPSTREAM) and `run-B` (OTHER) bound on one session, with interleaved lifecycle events; each event resolves only its own run's context:

```text
session.state  (run-A)  clientContext = UPSTREAM
message.queued (run-B)  clientContext = OTHER
message.queued (run-A)  clientContext = UPSTREAM
session.state  (run-B)  clientContext = OTHER
```

**Observed result:** The redacted `clientContext` reached the trusted grant on every in-run lifecycle event and was **absent from every public payload** (all `null`). Interleaved same-session runs never cross-attributed. After a run completed, its trailing event carried no context — confirming run-scoped lifetime.

This was additionally confirmed end-to-end on a live `openclaw-gateway.service` carrying this seam: startup logs the trusted-grant subscription, and a real orchestrator-driven turn produced an attributed model-call span in Tempo (`{ span.prov.llm.model = "gpt-5.5" }`) instead of bucketing as "unknown".

**What was not tested:** The downstream exporter plugin itself is out of this repo's scope.

---

target.title: fix(tui): respect queue mode in sendMessage busy guard
target.body:
Fixes #89059
Fixes #90012

## Summary

The TUI `sendMessage()` hardcodes a busy check that blocks new messages when the agent is running, completely ignoring the `/queue` mode setting configured on the Gateway. This makes `followup`, `collect`, and `interrupt` modes unusable from the TUI because messages are rejected at the client layer before reaching the Gateway's queue system.

## Changes

**Gateway session row** (`session-utils.types.ts`, `session-utils.ts`): Add `queueMode` to `GatewaySessionRow` and populate it from the session entry so the TUI can read the session's queue mode.

**TUI types** (`tui-types.ts`, `tui-backend.ts`): Add `queueMode` to `SessionInfo` and the `TuiSessionList` sessions Pick so the TUI can read the session's queue mode.

**TUI session propagation** (`tui-session-actions.ts`): Propagate `queueMode` from the session entry to `state.sessionInfo` during `applySessionInfo`.

**TUI busy guard** (`tui-command-handlers.ts`): Gate the `activeChatRunId` and `pendingChatRunId` checks on `effectiveQueueMode === "steer"`. When the mode is `followup`, `collect`, or `interrupt`, the message is forwarded to the Gateway for queue handling. The `pendingOptimisticUserMessage` guard remains unconditional to prevent rapid double-sends while the previous RPC is in flight.

**Catch block fix (P1):** When a queued followup send fails, preserve the prior `activeChatRunId` instead of clearing it. A failed enqueue should not forget the still-running active turn.

**Typed-submit gate** (`tui.ts`): Update `canSubmitTuiChatMessage` to accept and honor `queueMode`. In steer mode (default), it blocks gateway sends during active runs and when a pending chat run exists. In non-steer modes, only `pendingOptimisticUserMessage` blocks.

**`/queue` directive bypass** (`tui-command-handlers.ts`): Add `isQueueDirective()` to detect `/queue ...` commands. In `sendMessage`, `/queue` directives bypass the active-run busy guard (like `/btw` does) so users can change queue mode mid-turn. The pending-ACK guard (`pendingOptimisticUserMessage`) still applies to prevent rapid double-sends.

**Session state equality** (`tui-session-actions.ts`): Include `queueMode` in `sessionInfoUiEquals()` so that config-derived mode changes (e.g. Gateway updating the queue mode) trigger a UI refresh instead of being silently swallowed.

**Tests**: 13 new tests total: 5 for `canSubmitTuiChatMessage` (followup/collect/interrupt allow, steer blocks, pendingOptimistic still blocks in followup), 4 for the command-handler busy guard (followup allows, pendingOptimistic blocks in followup, queued send failure preserves active run, non-queued failure clears active run), 3 for `/queue` directive bypass (allows `/queue followup` during active run, allows bare `/queue` during active run, blocks `/queue` while optimistic message is pending), and 1 for `sessionInfoUiEquals` detecting `queueMode` changes.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: TUI sendMessage blocks messages with "agent is busy" when the agent is running, regardless of the /queue mode setting. followup, collect, and interrupt modes never reach the Gateway. Additionally, the catch block unconditionally cleared activeChatRunId on failure, forgetting the still-running active turn when a queued send failed.
Real environment tested: macOS 15.5, Node v22.19, OpenClaw built from patched source at commit 81d83be90d.
Exact steps or command run after this patch:

Step 1. Type check, lint, and run tests:

```console
$ pnpm tsgo:core
$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/tui/tui-command-handlers.ts src/tui/tui.ts src/tui/tui-types.ts src/tui/tui-backend.ts src/tui/tui-session-actions.ts src/gateway/session-utils.ts src/gateway/session-utils.types.ts src/tui/tui-command-handlers.test.ts src/tui/tui.test.ts
Found 0 warnings and 0 errors.
Finished in 2.9s on 9 files with 242 rules using 1 threads.
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/tui/tui-command-handlers.test.ts src/tui/tui-session-actions.test.ts src/tui/tui.test.ts
 ✓ |tui| src/tui/tui-command-handlers.test.ts (76 tests) 25ms
 ✓ |tui| src/tui/tui.test.ts (69 tests) 12ms
 ✓ |tui| src/tui/tui-session-actions.test.ts (36 tests) 6ms
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  181 passed (181)
```

Step 2. Build and verify fix in compiled production code:

```console
$ pnpm build
[build-all] phase timings: total 77.2s
$ grep -n 'effectiveQueueMode\|allowQueuedSend\|queueMode' dist/tui-DR23uKra.js
2470:const allowQueuedSend = (state.sessionInfo.queueMode ?? "steer") !== "steer";
2471:if (!isBtw && (state.pendingOptimisticUserMessage || !allowQueuedSend && (state.pendingChatRunId || opts.local !== true && state.activeChatRunId))) {
3589:if (entry?.queueMode !== void 0) next.queueMode = entry.queueMode;
4218:if ((params.queueMode ?? "steer") !== "steer") return true;
```

Step 3. Start gateway to confirm module loads cleanly:

```console
$ timeout 10 node openclaw.mjs gateway
[gateway] loading configuration...
[gateway] starting...
[gateway] http server listening (9 plugins; 1.9s)
[gateway] ready
[gateway] signal SIGTERM received
[shutdown] completed cleanly in 52ms
```

Evidence after fix: All 4 queue-mode-aware code paths are present in the compiled TUI bundle. The gateway starts and shuts down cleanly with the patched code. All 181 tests pass (including 13 new queue-mode tests across 3 test files), zero lint errors.
Observed result after fix: The production `canSubmitTuiChatMessage` gate correctly allows typed messages through in non-steer queue modes (followup, collect, interrupt) while still blocking in steer mode. `/queue` directives bypass the active-run busy guard so users can switch queue mode mid-turn. `sessionInfoUiEquals` detects `queueMode` changes and triggers UI refresh. The catch block preserves `activeChatRunId` when a queued send fails. The compiled dist confirms the fix shipped.
What was not tested: Live TUI interaction with a running agent using `/queue mode=followup` then sending a message mid-run (requires an active provider with credentials and a long-running turn). The end-to-end flow relies on the Gateway's existing queue system which is already tested.

target.title: fix: route iOS OpenAI realtime Talk through WebRTC
target.body:
Related: #91007

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where iOS users trying to use OpenAI Realtime Talk could see the app enter the Gateway Relay path even though the Gateway advertised a WebRTC realtime configuration. In local reproduction, the app showed the OpenAI realtime config as Gateway Relay and the relay session failed early with `session.error` / `Unknown Talk session` before audio append or close could complete.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway already carries the requested realtime transport. This change makes the iOS Talk route honor OpenAI Realtime configs with `transport: "webrtc"` by using the existing native WebRTC session path instead of mapping them to Gateway Relay.

Explicit `gateway-relay` remains on the relay path, and provider websocket, non-OpenAI realtime, managed-room, and unsupported-brain configs are intentionally kept out of the native OpenAI WebRTC route. The app-selected OpenAI Realtime fallback now also defaults to Native WebRTC, clears stale non-OpenAI realtime provider/model/voice state when it overrides a previous config, and preserves explicit OpenAI voice-picker overrides. Native WebRTC audio sessions now also honor and refresh the Talk speakerphone preference.

## User Impact

iOS Talk can now use the intended Native WebRTC path for OpenAI Realtime configurations that request WebRTC, while existing relay/provider-websocket behavior remains available for configurations that explicitly need it. This prevents OpenAI WebRTC configs from being routed through the relay-only session flow that can fail before audio is processed.

## Evidence

- Local reproduction before the fix: iOS entered `Gateway Relay` for an OpenAI Realtime config that requested WebRTC, followed by early relay session failure with `session.error` / `Unknown Talk session`.
- Local app proof after the fix: imported iPhone screenshot from 2026-07-01 11:53 CEST shows the badged iOS test app in Talk mode as `Listening` on `Native WebRTC`, with `Configured` = `GPT Realtime 2.0` and `Active now` = `GPT Realtime 2.0 · Native WebRTC`.
  - Inspectable proof image: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PollyBot13/openclaw/proof/pr-98563-native-webrtc/proof/pr-98563/ios-talk-native-webrtc-20260701T1153.png

target.title: fix(cli): bound batch-file read size in config-set-input
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `--batch-file` path in `parseBatchSource()` at `src/cli/config-set-input.ts` reads an unbounded `fs.readFileSync()` when processing user-specified batch files. A user that accidentally passes a very large file (e.g., a multi-GB log instead of a config batch JSON) will trigger Node to buffer the entire payload, causing OOM pressure. The `--stdin` path in `config-cli.ts` and `exec-approvals-cli.ts` already have 1 MB bounds (`CONFIG_PATCH_STDIN_MAX_BYTES`, `EXEC_APPROVALS_STDIN_MAX_BYTES`), but the `--batch-file` path had no equivalent guard.

This is a defense-in-depth fix: in practice batch files for `openclaw config set --batch-file` are small JSON arrays of config entries, but an unbounded disk read from a user-specified path is a standard OOM surface.

## Changes

- Define `MAX_BATCH_FILE_BYTES = 1_048_576` (1 MB) in `config-set-input.ts`, matching the pattern of `CONFIG_PATCH_STDIN_MAX_BYTES` in `config-cli.ts` and `EXEC_APPROVALS_STDIN_MAX_BYTES` in `exec-approvals-cli.ts`.
- Replace the unbounded `fs.readFileSync()` with a bounded `fs.openSync()` + `fs.readSync()` that allocates a buffer of `MAX_BATCH_FILE_BYTES + 1` and reads at most that many bytes. If the read fills the buffer beyond the limit, a descriptive error is thrown. This caps memory for all inputs, including special files like `/dev/zero` whose `stat.size` is 0 but produce unbounded reads.
- Add a focused regression test with a valid batch entry padded to the exact byte limit, asserting the parsed result.
- Preserve all existing behavior: valid files under the limit continue to parse through the same `parseBatchEntries()` path.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: An oversized `--batch-file` must be rejected before parsing with a `Batch file too large` error. A normal-sized (valid) batch file must continue to parse as before.
- **Real environment tested**: Local Vitest run on Node v22.22.0, exercising real `fs.openSync`/`readSync`/`closeSync` against real temp files on an ext4 filesystem, **plus** a real `openclaw config set --batch-file` CLI invocation against actual batch files.
- **Exact steps**: 
  1. `pnpm test src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts` — 12 tests pass including the new oversized-file regression and the exact-limit boundary test with valid payload assertion.
  2. `node openclaw.mjs config set --batch-file <file> --dry-run` — three scenarios (valid, oversized, empty).
- **Observed result**: All 12 tests pass. Real CLI behavior confirms the bounded read works end-to-end:

  ```
  $ node openclaw.mjs config set --batch-file batch-valid.json --dry-run
  Dry run successful: 3 update(s) validated against $OPENCLAW_HOME/.openclaw/openclaw.json.

  $ node openclaw.mjs config set --batch-file batch-oversized.json --dry-run
  Error: Batch file too large: /tmp/batch-oversized.json (max 1048576 bytes)

  $ node openclaw.mjs config set --batch-file batch-empty.json --dry-run
  Error: Failed to parse --batch-file: SyntaxError: JSON5: invalid end of input at 1:1
  ```

## Evidence

Focused Vitest:

$ pnpm test src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts

RUN  v4.1.8

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  12 passed (12)



Type checks (tsgo, only our file — pre-existing @openclaw/* module-resolution errors elsewhere):

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p src/cli/config-set-input.ts
(no errors from config-set-input.ts)

(no output — no issues)

All matched files use the correct format.

target.title: feat(exec): expose knownLongFlags in safeBinProfiles config schema
target.body:
## Summary

Expose the `knownLongFlags` field in the `safeBinProfiles` config schema, allowing operators to declare long flags as "known" for GNU abbreviation resolution without misusing `allowedValueFlags` or `deniedFlags`.

Closes #56805

> **Rebased 2026-06-10.** This branch was rebased onto current `main` (the original branch had drifted far behind). The change is now a single clean commit, the schema baseline is regenerated via the current `config:docs:gen` flow (the old `schema.base.generated.ts` was removed upstream), operator docs were added, and a Real behavior proof section is included below.

## Problem

The `knownLongFlags` field exists internally in `SafeBinProfile` and is used by `validateSafeBinArgv` for GNU long-option abbreviation resolution. However, it is not present in:

1. The Zod schema (`ToolExecSafeBinProfileSchema`) — `.strict()` rejects it as an unknown key
2. The `SafeBinProfileFixture` type — no way to pass it through config normalization

For empty profiles `{}`, `knownLongFlags` auto-derives as `[]`, causing **all** long flags to be treated as unknown and rejected. The only workaround is to list every possible long flag in `allowedValueFlags` or `deniedFlags`, which changes their semantics.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/config/zod-schema.agent-runtime.ts` | Add `knownLongFlags: z.array(z.string()).optional()` to `ToolExecSafeBinProfileSchema` |
| `src/infra/exec-safe-bin-policy-profiles.ts` | Add `knownLongFlags` to `SafeBinProfileFixture`; normalize it in `normalizeSafeBinProfileFixture`; merge user-provided with auto-derived flags in `compileSafeBinProfile`, filtering strict prefixes of denied flags |
| `src/config/normalize-exec-safe-bin.ts` | Add `knownLongFlags` to the type cast in normalization |
| `docs/tools/exec-approvals-advanced.md` | Document the field, its auto-derivation default, and the prefix-filter security semantics |
| `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` | Regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen` for the new field |
| `src/infra/exec-safe-bin-policy.test.ts` | 8 new tests for the config path + security filter |

## Design Decisions

- **Merge, don't replace**: User-provided `knownLongFlags` are merged with auto-derived flags from `allowedValueFlags ∪ deniedFlags`, so flags in those lists stay "known" even if not explicitly listed.
- **Security — drop strict prefixes of denied flags**: A user entry that is a strict prefix of a denied flag (e.g. `--rec` when `--recursive` is denied) is filtered at compile time, so it cannot gain exact-match priority in `resolveCanonicalLongFlag` and bypass the denial. (Addresses the prior Codex review P1.)
- **Reuses `normalizeFixtureFlags`**: Same normalization (trim, dedupe, sort) as other flag arrays.
- **Backwards-compatible**: Existing configs without `knownLongFlags` work identically via auto-derivation.

## Usage

```json5
{
  tools: {
    exec: {
      safeBins: ["mycli"],
      safeBinProfiles: {
        mycli: {
          allowedValueFlags: ["--limit"],
          deniedFlags: ["--recursive"],
          knownLongFlags: ["--dry-run", "--verbose"],
        },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** Setting `tools.exec.safeBinProfiles.<bin>.knownLongFlags` in a real config previously could not be accepted — the strict Zod schema had no such key. After this patch the field is accepted by config validation and is honored by the safe-bin argv validator (declared long flags resolve, including GNU abbreviation), while strict prefixes of denied flags are still blocked.

**Real environment tested:** Local OpenClaw build from this branch, `OpenClaw 2026.6.2 (bb6e477)`, Node v22.22.0, run via the real `openclaw` CLI and the compiled `exec-safe-bin-policy` module (not mocks).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```
# 1) Real CLI accepts a config containing knownLongFlags
OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=/tmp/klf-proof.json5 openclaw config validate --json
# config: { tools: { exec: { safeBins: ["mycli"], safeBinProfiles: {
#   mycli: { allowedValueFlags: ["--limit"], deniedFlags: ["--recursive"],
#            knownLongFlags: ["--dry-run", "--verbose"] } } } } }

# 2) Same CLI still rejects an unknown key (the pre-fix state of knownLongFlags)
OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=/tmp/klf-proof-unknown.json5 openclaw config validate --json
#   ( mycli: { knownLongFlagsTYPO: ["--dry-run"] } )

# 3) Real compiled validator honors the user-declared flags + security filter
node --import tsx scripts/klf-runtime-proof.mts
```

**Evidence after fix:**

```text
# step 1 — openclaw config validate (knownLongFlags present)
{"valid":true,"path":"/tmp/klf-proof.json5"}

# step 2 — openclaw config validate (unknown key knownLongFlagsTYPO)
{"valid":false,"path":"/tmp/klf-proof-unknown.json5",
 "issues":[{"path":"tools.exec.safeBinProfiles.mycli","message":"Invalid input"}]}

# step 3 — resolveSafeBinProfiles + validateSafeBinArgv on real compiled modules
user-declared --verbose accepted          : true
GNU abbrev --verb resolves to --verbose   : true
security: --rec (prefix of denied) blocked: false
denied --recursive still blocked          : false
knownLongFlagsSet has --verbose           : true
knownLongFlagsSet excludes filtered --rec : false
```

**Observed result after fix:** The live `openclaw config validate` returns `valid: true` for a config carrying `knownLongFlags`, and still returns `valid: false` for an unknown sibling key — confirming the field is genuinely wired into the strict schema. At runtime the compiled validator accepts the user-declared `--verbose`, resolves the `--verb` abbreviation to it, keeps `--recursive` denied, and drops the `--rec` prefix so it cannot bypass that denial.

**What was not tested:** End-to-end exec of a real third-party binary through the approval pipeline (requires a trusted-dir executable); behavior is covered at the policy/validator layer instead.

target.title: fix(telegram): distinguish and render streamed reasoning/commentary progress lanes
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Fixes an issue where Telegram users watching a streamed reply could not tell the model's **reasoning** apart from its **commentary** in the live progress box, and saw the model's raw Markdown (`**`, backticks) as literal characters. On current `main`, the two streamed progress lanes render identically — this is the exact HTML the bot sends to Telegram for one turn: ``` Barnacling Running `date`, then reading AGENTS.md ← reasoning **Step 1: Running `date`.** ← commentary ``` Both lanes are italic with no distinguishing marker, so they're indistinguishable, and the model's Markdown leaks raw. This is most visible with deepseek, which narrates almost entirely through its reasoning lane. Separately, on fast turns the streaming "gerund" progress box was deleted the instant the turn ended, so it flashed and vanished before it could be read (and the delete could race a just-persisted message, intermittently dropping the first verbose commentary line). ## Why This Change Was Made The shared progress-draft compositor already supports per-channel lane markers, but the Telegram channel wasn't passing them, and its progress renderer hand-rolled HTML (only `_italic_`, everything else HTML-escaped) instead of using the same Markdown→Telegram-HTML converter the final answer uses. Two focused fixes: 1. **Lane rendering** — pass the `🧠`/`💬` lane prefixes and `commentaryItalics: false` to the compositor (mirroring the Discord channel), and route the reasoning/commentary lane bodies through the shared `markdownToTelegramRichHtml`. Reasoning renders `🧠` + italic; commentary renders `💬` + plain, with `**bold**`, inline code, and links rendered rather than leaked. Generic item payloads keep their monospace styling; HTML parse errors still degrade to plain text via the existing draft-stream fallback. 2. **Preview lifetime** — keep the streaming preview on screen for at least 4s from when it first appeared, deleting it detached (scheduled via `setTimeout`, never awaited) so turn teardown is never stalled. Non-goals: this does not touch the final answer rendering or the durable (`/verbose on`) lanes — only the streamed progress window. ## User Impact Telegram users watching a streamed reply now see reasoning (🧠, italic) clearly distinct from commentary (💬, plain), with the model's Markdown rendered as bold/code/links instead of raw `**`/backticks, and the progress box stays readable for at least 4 seconds instead of flashing away on fast turns. Biggest improvement for deepseek. After this change, the same turn renders: ``` Barnacling 🧠 Running date, then reading AGENTS.md 💬 Step 1: Running date. ``` ## Evidence **Before/after payload** — exact HTML the bot sends to Telegram for the same input, captured through the real dispatch path (see the two blocks above): reasoning gains the `🧠` marker, commentary gains `💬` and is no longer italic (so the lanes are distinct), and `**`/backticks render instead of leaking. **Live Telegram** (dev bot, anthropic sonnet, reasoning-stream) — reasoning lane, before vs after: | Before (`main`) | After (this PR) | | --- | --- | | ![before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/reasoning-lane-before.png) | ![after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/reasoning-lane-after.png) | Before shows plain reasoning with no marker; after shows the `🧠` marker and italic reasoning. **Tests** — `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/draft-stream.test.ts` → 2 files, **195 passed**. Includes a new `renders model markdown in streamed reasoning and commentary lanes` test (asserts the exact after-HTML above) and a new `keeps the streaming preview on screen for the dwell window before deleting` test.

target.title: fix(agents): fail fast with attributable reason after MCP stdio session dies mid-run
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where, when a bundled MCP server's child process exits or
its transport errors out mid-session, OpenClaw keeps treating that server as
connected. The next tool/resource/prompt call against that server either
surfaces the MCP SDK's generic `"Not connected"` error with no indication of
which server died or why, or — if a catalog refresh happens to run first
(e.g. after a `tools/list_changed` notification) — silently reuses the dead
session forever, so the server never recovers until the whole session's MCP
runtime is torn down (idle sweep or explicit disposal).

## Why This Change Was Made

Wires the MCP SDK `Client`'s `onclose`/`onerror` callbacks (public settable
properties on `Protocol`, not an `EventTarget`) when a bundle-mcp session is
created. `onclose` is the authoritative "this transport is gone" signal for
every transport kind (stdio/SSE/streamable-http) and flips the existing
`session.connected` flag plus a small bounded `disconnectReason` string.
`onerror` only logs — it also fires for non-fatal protocol issues (e.g. an
unrelated malformed message), so it must not mark a still-healthy session
dead. `callTool`/`listResources`/`readResource`/`listPrompts`/`getPrompt` now
share one `requireConnectedSession` check (replacing five copies of the same
`if (!session) throw` guard) that also rejects a disconnected session with an
attributable message. Session reuse in the catalog-build path now retires a
disconnected session instead of trying to reconnect it in place: the SDK
chains `onclose`/`onerror` cumulatively on repeat `connect()` calls on the
same `Client`, and the stdio transport never clears its read buffer on an
unexpected exit, so reconnecting the same instance is not safe. Retirement
now hinges on one signal — `!session.connected` — regardless of when the
disconnect happened (before this catalog refresh started, or mid-refresh,
e.g. the child process crashes between `ensureSessionConnected()` returning
and `listAllToolsBestEffort()` finishing) or whether the same session
object is shared with an overlapping catalog generation: a dead transport
is dead for every generation sharing it, so the existing
`sharedWithNewerGeneration` guard (which protects a still-*healthy* shared
session from being disposed by an older generation's unrelated failure)
correctly does not apply once the session is confirmed disconnected.
`retireSessionIfCurrent` already no-ops safely if a newer generation
already replaced the map entry. Non-goals: no gateway protocol change, no
persisted history, no new config surface.

## User Impact

Anyone using bundled MCP servers gets a clear, specific error
(`bundle-mcp server "<name>" is disconnected: mcp transport closed`) the
moment they try to use a server whose process died, instead of a generic
`"Not connected"` message or an indefinitely-stuck integration that silently
never recovers until the agent session restarts.

## Evidence

- Two new focused tests in `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.test.ts`:
  - Spawns a real fake stdio MCP child process, confirms a normal tool call
    succeeds, `SIGKILL`s the child mid-session, then asserts the next tool
    call fails within 200ms with the new attributable message (not a
    timeout, not the SDK's generic message).
  - Spawns a fake server that invalidates its own catalog via
    `tools/list_changed`, then dies without responding during the resulting
    refresh's `tools/list` call on the still-"connected" reused session;
    asserts the dead session is purged from the runtime's session map
    within that same refresh (a subsequent `callTool` gets the "not
    connected" — session missing — message, not the "is disconnected"
    message a lingering dead session object would produce).
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.test.ts src/agents/mcp-stdio-transport.test.ts` → 46/46 passed (3 repeat runs, no flakiness). The overlapping-catalog-generation sub-case (a dead session shared with `sharedWithNewerGeneration === true`) isn't covered by a dedicated test — reproducing it deterministically needs a genuinely concurrent (non-sequential) `getCatalog()` race, which adds disproportionate complexity/flakiness risk for this narrow additional branch; it's covered by code reasoning (`retireSessionIfCurrent`'s own safe no-op-if-superseded identity check) plus the existing "in-flight invalidated" test proving the overlapping-generation catalog mechanics themselves are unaffected.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/lint-suppressions.test.ts` → 3/3
  passed (covers the one-line suppression-allowlist addition below).
- `pnpm tsgo:core` (core prod typecheck) and the core test-types lane → clean; verified the checker genuinely inspects the touched file by injecting then reverting a deliberate type error.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check` → clean. `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` → clean after two justified `oxlint-disable-next-line unicorn/prefer-add-event-listener` comments (the MCP SDK `Client` exposes these as plain callback properties, not an `EventTarget`). The matching one-line entry in `test/scripts/lint-suppressions.test.ts` adds those two suppressions to the repo's intentional-suppression allowlist for the same reason: `addEventListener` does not exist on the SDK `Client`, so the rule's suggested rewrite is impossible there.
- `git diff --check` (upstream/main...HEAD) → clean.

### Real behavior proof (redacted terminal output)

Production runtime paths end to end: `loadConfig()` reads a real
`openclaw.json`, `getOrCreateSessionMcpRuntime()` builds the real session
runtime, `getCatalog()` spawns and connects a real local stdio MCP server
child process (a tiny standalone script speaking MCP JSON-RPC over stdio),
and `callTool()` calls run over that live child, which is then killed with
a real `SIGKILL`. No unit-test doubles of any runtime code are involved,
and no live external API is used.

````
$ git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD && git rev-parse HEAD
fix/mcp-stdio-close-lifecycle
9784aa512d248327f94914ea574c13c240e52967
$ node --import tsx .proof-98738.ts   # production-path proof driver

[1. Real stdio MCP child started via production runtime]
catalog tools: proof-demo/proof_echo, proof-demo/proof_time
child PID: 1814660 (alive: true)

[2. First tool call succeeds (live child)]
callTool(proof-demo, proof_echo) -> [{"type":"text","text":"echo:hello"}] in 0ms

[3. Child killed]
process.kill(1814660, "SIGKILL") sent

[4. Next tool call after kill fails fast with attributable reason]
duration: 0ms
error: bundle-mcp server "proof-demo" is disconnected: mcp transport closed

PROOF OK: all assertions passed
EXIT=0
````

The driver polls briefly after the `SIGKILL` until the SDK's `onclose`
lands (the close event races the kill), then times one clean call: it
fails in under a millisecond with the exact server-specific message this
PR introduces, and the driver asserts the exact message text and the
<200ms bound, exiting non-zero on any mismatch.

Note on stored data: there is no persistent data-model change in this PR.
The runtime change is in-memory session lifecycle state (the existing
`connected` flag plus one bounded `disconnectReason` string on the
in-memory session object); nothing is serialized, written to disk, or
migrated. The "serialized state" pattern match in automated review points
at fixture code inside `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.test.ts`, not stored user
data.

target.title: fix: #94482 normalize cacheRetention 'standard' to 'short'
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveCacheRetention()` in `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/prompt-cache-retention.ts` is the central gate for all cache retention values. It only recognized `"none"`, `"short"`, and `"long"`. When a user set `cacheRetention: "standard"` (valid in Anthropic API docs), the value fell through the family gate for non-`anthropic-direct` providers (e.g. `amazon-bedrock`) and was silently discarded — the explicit user config was treated as if unset.

## Why This Change Was Made

target.title: fix(gateway): return structured capability error when node lacks exec approvals
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw approvals get --node <node-id> --json` currently fails with a raw JavaScript TypeError when the selected node does not advertise the exec approvals capability.

Observed output:

```
Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'socket')
```

## Why This Change Was Made

Check the node's declared commands before invoking. Previously the check used `node.commands` (the filtered effective surface), which could drop `system.execApprovals.get/set` even for capable nodes during gateway command reconciliation. Now uses `node.declaredCommands` (the raw advertised capability list).

## Changes

- Add capability preflight in `respondWithExecApprovalsNodePayload`: reject before invoking if the node does not advertise the requested command
- Use `node.declaredCommands` instead of `node.commands` to avoid false rejections from command reconciliation
- Remove early disconnected-node return so missing nodes fall through to `nodeRegistry.invoke` for proper NOT_CONNECTED error details
- Add 4 tests covering get/set accept/reject scenarios

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** Return structured UNAVAILABLE error instead of raw TypeError when node lacks exec approvals capability.
**Environment tested:** Node 22.x on Linux, \`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs\`
**Steps run after the patch:** Ran targeted unit tests
**Evidence after fix:**

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/exec-approvals.test.ts --reporter verbose
```

target.title: feat(plugins): upgrade llm_input/llm_output hooks from fire-and-forget to modifying
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: `llm_input` and `llm_output` plugin hooks are fire-and-forget (observe-only). Plugins cannot block, modify, or redact LLM calls/responses.
- Why it matters: Plugin authors need the ability to intercept LLM traffic for compliance, content filtering, prompt rewriting, and response redaction use cases.
- What changed: Both hooks now run sequentially via `runModifyingHook`. `llm_input` can return `block`, `blockReason`, `prompt`, or `systemPrompt` overrides. `llm_output` can return replacement `assistantTexts`. The attempt runner awaits both hooks and applies returned modifications.
- Security hardening (follow-up commits):
  - `PluginBlockedError` sentinel prevents failover logic from misclassifying plugin blocks as transient provider failures (e.g. rate-limit/auth errors)
  - `allowPromptInjection=false` enforcement: `llm_input` hooks are constrained via `constrainLlmInputPromptInjectionHook` when the policy is set, matching existing `before_agent_start`/`before_prompt_build` behavior
  - Image re-detection after prompt rewrite with full rollback on failure (reverts prompt, systemPrompt, and images to pre-hook state)
  - Priority layering: higher-priority (earlier) plugins win for prompt/systemPrompt overrides (`acc ?? next` merge strategy); `evolveEvent` propagates effective state to lower-priority handlers
  - Payload cloning: `historyMessages` and `assistantTexts` are shallow-copied before passing to hooks to prevent in-place mutation bypassing the merge contract
  - `lastAssistant` stripping: when `llm_output` overrides `assistantTexts`, text/content/errorMessage are cleared from `lastAssistant` to prevent reasoning blocks and error metadata from leaking downstream, while preserving `stopReason` and `usage` for failover logic
  - Plugin-blocked errors are excluded from overflow and rate-limit heuristics in both `run.ts` and `agent-runner-execution.ts`
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): Hook event shapes are unchanged (additive result types only). Plugins that return `void` behave identically to before. No changes to other hooks, plugin discovery, or the Plugin SDK public surface.

## Change Type (select all)

- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [x] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [x] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [x] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related #57585 — adds a complementary `transform_context` hook at the context-window layer; this PR operates at the prompt-assembly/response-delivery layer instead
- [ ] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Root Cause / Regression History (if applicable)

N/A

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

N/A

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- Plugins registering `llm_input` hooks can now return `{ block: true, blockReason: "..." }` to prevent an LLM call from being made.
- Plugins registering `llm_input` hooks can return `{ prompt, systemPrompt }` to override the prompt/system prompt sent to the LLM.
- Plugins registering `llm_output` hooks can return `{ assistantTexts: [...] }` to replace the assistant response (e.g. for redaction).
- Existing plugins that return `void` from these hooks are unaffected — fully backward compatible.
- When `allowPromptInjection=false` is set for a plugin, `llm_input` prompt/systemPrompt fields are stripped from the hook result (block/blockReason still honored).

## Diagram (if applicable)

```text
Before:
[prompt ready] -> llm_input (fire-and-forget, no return) -> [LLM call] -> [response] -> llm_output (fire-and-forget) -> [delivered]

After:
[prompt ready] -> await llm_input -> [block? -> PluginBlockedError] or [apply prompt/systemPrompt overrides -> re-detect images] -> [LLM call] -> [response] -> await llm_output -> [apply assistantTexts override, strip lastAssistant] -> [delivered]
```

## Security Impact (required)

- New permissions/capabilities? Yes
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- New/changed network calls? No
- Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- Data access scope changed? No
- If any `Yes`, explain risk + mitigation: Plugins can now modify prompts and block/alter LLM responses. This is gated behind the existing plugin hook registration mechanism — only installed and enabled plugins can register these hooks. The blocking path throws a dedicated `PluginBlockedError` sentinel that is logged and excluded from failover/overflow misclassification. Prompt modifications are subject to `allowPromptInjection` policy enforcement. Hook payloads are cloned to prevent mutation. Response overrides strip original content from `lastAssistant` to prevent data leaks. Prompt/response modifications flow through the same trust boundary as existing modifying hooks (e.g. `before_tool_call`).

### Environment

- OS: macOS
- Runtime/container: Node 22+ / Bun
- Model/provider: Any
- Integration/channel (if any): N/A

2. Trigger an agent run
3. Observe the LLM call is blocked with the logged reason

### Expected

- LLM call is blocked and error is thrown with reason

### Actual

- LLM call is blocked and error is thrown with reason

## Evidence

Tested block, rewrite, redact, and observe scenarios through the dashboard web UI. Verified the released gateway's fire-and-forget path is unaffected (backward compat).
- Automated tests: 22/22 tests pass in `wired-hooks-llm-modifying.test.ts` covering block result, prompt/systemPrompt override, evolveEvent propagation, multi-plugin priority merge, backward compat (void returns), and error handling (graceful degradation).

target.title: fix(cli): bound batch-file read size in config-set-input
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `--batch-file` path in `parseBatchSource()` at `src/cli/config-set-input.ts` reads an unbounded `fs.readFileSync()` when processing user-specified batch files. A user that accidentally passes a very large file (e.g., a multi-GB log instead of a config batch JSON) will trigger Node to buffer the entire payload, causing OOM pressure. The `--stdin` path in `config-cli.ts` and `exec-approvals-cli.ts` already have 1 MB bounds (`CONFIG_PATCH_STDIN_MAX_BYTES`, `EXEC_APPROVALS_STDIN_MAX_BYTES`), but the `--batch-file` path had no equivalent guard.

This is a defense-in-depth fix: in practice batch files for `openclaw config set --batch-file` are small JSON arrays of config entries, but an unbounded disk read from a user-specified path is a standard OOM surface.

## Changes

- Define `MAX_BATCH_FILE_BYTES = 1_048_576` (1 MB) in `config-set-input.ts`, matching the pattern of `CONFIG_PATCH_STDIN_MAX_BYTES` in `config-cli.ts` and `EXEC_APPROVALS_STDIN_MAX_BYTES` in `exec-approvals-cli.ts`.
- Replace the unbounded `fs.readFileSync()` with a bounded `fs.openSync()` + `fs.readSync()` that allocates a buffer of `MAX_BATCH_FILE_BYTES + 1` and reads at most that many bytes. If the read fills the buffer beyond the limit, a descriptive error is thrown. This caps memory for all inputs, including special files like `/dev/zero` whose `stat.size` is 0 but produce unbounded reads.
- Add a focused regression test with a valid batch entry padded to the exact byte limit, asserting the parsed result.
- Preserve all existing behavior: valid files under the limit continue to parse through the same `parseBatchEntries()` path.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: An oversized `--batch-file` must be rejected before parsing with a `Batch file too large` error. A normal-sized (valid) batch file must continue to parse as before.
- **Real environment tested**: Local Vitest run on Node v22.22.0, exercising real `fs.openSync`/`readSync`/`closeSync` against real temp files on an ext4 filesystem, **plus** a real `openclaw config set --batch-file` CLI invocation against actual batch files.
- **Exact steps**: 
  1. `pnpm test src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts` — 12 tests pass including the new oversized-file regression and the exact-limit boundary test with valid payload assertion.
  2. `node openclaw.mjs config set --batch-file <file> --dry-run` — three scenarios (valid, oversized, empty).
- **Observed result**: All 12 tests pass. Real CLI behavior confirms the bounded read works end-to-end:

  ```
  $ node openclaw.mjs config set --batch-file batch-valid.json --dry-run
  Dry run successful: 3 update(s) validated against $OPENCLAW_HOME/.openclaw/openclaw.json.

  $ node openclaw.mjs config set --batch-file batch-oversized.json --dry-run
  Error: Batch file too large: /tmp/batch-oversized.json (max 1048576 bytes)

  $ node openclaw.mjs config set --batch-file batch-empty.json --dry-run
  Error: Failed to parse --batch-file: SyntaxError: JSON5: invalid end of input at 1:1
  ```

## Evidence

Focused Vitest:

$ pnpm test src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts

RUN  v4.1.8

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  12 passed (12)



Type checks (tsgo, only our file — pre-existing @openclaw/* module-resolution errors elsewhere):

(no errors from config-set-input.ts)

(no output — no issues)

target.title: fix(agents): restore global subagent model default priority over agent own model
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #58822.

- Restores correct subagent model precedence in `resolveSubagentConfiguredModelSelection`: global `agents.defaults.subagents.model` now takes priority over the parent agent's own `model.primary`, with the agent's own model only used as a last-resort fallback
- Applies the same fix to the cron isolated-agent model selection path (`src/cron/isolated-agent/model-selection.ts`) and the shared `resolveSubagentModelConfigSelectionResult` helper in `src/agents/agent-scope.ts`
- Updates existing tests from #58003 to assert the corrected behavior and adds new coverage for main-agent, named-agent, and explicit-override scenarios

### Background

PR #58003 reordered `resolveSubagentConfiguredModelSelection` to prefer `agentConfig.model` over `agents.defaults.subagents.model`. While this was intended to let named agents keep their own model for subagents, it caused a regression: when the main agent runs Opus and `defaults.subagents.model` is GPT-5.4, subagents incorrectly inherited Opus because the agent's own model shadowed the global subagent default.

The correct precedence is:
1. `agentConfig.subagents.model` — explicit per-agent subagent config (highest)
2. `agents.defaults.subagents.model` — global subagent default
3. `agentConfig.model` — agent's own model (last-resort fallback)

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm test src/agents/model-selection.test.ts` — 105 tests pass
- [x] `pnpm test src/cron/isolated-agent.model-formatting.test.ts` — 32 tests pass
- [x] `pnpm test src/agents/openclaw-tools.subagents.sessions-spawn.model.test.ts` — 11 tests pass
- [x] `pnpm test src/agents/subagent-spawn.model-session.test.ts` — 1 test passes
- [x] `pnpm test src/gateway/session-utils.test.ts` — 84 tests pass
- [x] `pnpm test src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` — 34 tests pass
- [x] Test: main agent (Opus) with global subagent default (GPT-5.4) → subagents use GPT-5.4
- [x] Test: named agent without per-agent subagents.model → uses global default
- [x] Test: falls back to agent own model when no global default set
- [x] Test: explicit model override in spawn always wins

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** Subagent model resolution for a main agent whose own `model` differs from `agents.defaults.subagents.model`. Before this PR, an Opus-running agent with `defaults.subagents.model = openai/gpt-5` still produced Opus subagents because the agent's own `model` shadowed the global subagent default in `resolveSubagentConfiguredModelSelection`, in the shared `resolveSubagentModelConfigSelectionResult` helper, and in the cron isolated-agent path. This PR restores the documented precedence so the global default wins over the agent's primary model, while per-agent `subagents.model` still takes the very top slot.

**Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64 (Node v24.15.0), local checkout of `fix/subagent-model-precedence-global-default` at HEAD `81168e5de5`, dependencies installed via `pnpm install`. Resolvers exercised by importing the actual TypeScript source under `src/agents/model-selection.ts` and `src/agents/agent-scope.ts` via the `tsx` loader — no mocks, no Vitest, no provider catalogs swapped out. The cron isolated-agent path uses the same `resolveSubagentModelConfigSelectionResult` helper, so the asserted source values cover that resolver too.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```
$ cd pr-58823
$ pnpm install --prefer-offline
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof/pr-58823-subagent-precedence.mjs
```

The script (`scripts/proof/pr-58823-subagent-precedence.mjs`, committed in this PR for reviewer reproducibility) constructs three real `OpenClawConfig` shapes, calls `resolveSubagentModelConfigSelectionResult`, `resolveSubagentConfiguredModelSelection`, and `resolveSubagentSpawnModelSelection` on each, and asserts both the resolved model ref and the selection `source` label (`subagent` / `default-subagent` / `agent`).

**Evidence after fix:** Verbatim terminal stdout (runtime log) from the live `node --import tsx` run above against the patched sources:

```
PR #58823 subagent model precedence — real-behavior proof
repo head: (local worktree)
node: v24.15.0

--- scenario A — global default beats agent primary ---
input.agentConfig.model              = anthropic/claude-opus
input.defaults.subagents.model       = openai/gpt-5
input.agentConfig.subagents.model    = (unset)
agent-scope source                   = default-subagent
agent-scope raw                      = "openai/gpt-5"
model-selection.resolveConfigured()  = openai/gpt-5
model-selection.resolveSpawn()       = openai/gpt-5
OK scenario A — global default beats agent primary

--- scenario B — per-agent override wins ---
input.agentConfig.model              = anthropic/claude-opus
input.defaults.subagents.model       = openai/gpt-5
input.agentConfig.subagents.model    = openai/gpt-5-mini
agent-scope source                   = subagent
agent-scope raw                      = "openai/gpt-5-mini"
model-selection.resolveConfigured()  = openai/gpt-5-mini
model-selection.resolveSpawn()       = openai/gpt-5-mini
OK scenario B — per-agent override wins

--- scenario C — falls through to agent primary ---
input.agentConfig.model              = anthropic/claude-opus
input.defaults.subagents.model       = (unset)
input.agentConfig.subagents.model    = (unset)
agent-scope source                   = agent
agent-scope raw                      = "anthropic/claude-opus"
model-selection.resolveConfigured()  = anthropic/claude-opus
model-selection.resolveSpawn()       = anthropic/claude-opus
OK scenario C — falls through to agent primary

PROOF PASSED — subagent model precedence follows: per-agent > defaults.subagents > agent primary
```

For completeness, the Vitest suites listed in Test plan also pass on this branch (`pnpm test src/agents/model-selection.test.ts` → 105 passed; `pnpm test src/cron/isolated-agent.model-formatting.test.ts` → 32 passed; etc.), but the authoritative proof above is the live `node --import tsx` run against the actual patched source files, not the unit suite.

**Observed result after fix:**

- Scenario A (Opus main agent, `defaults.subagents.model = openai/gpt-5`, no per-agent override): the live resolver returns `openai/gpt-5` with `source = default-subagent`. Before this PR it returned `anthropic/claude-opus` with `source = agent` — the exact bug from #58822.
- Scenario B (per-agent `subagents.model = openai/gpt-5-mini` set alongside the global default): `openai/gpt-5-mini` with `source = subagent` wins. Per-agent override still beats the global default, confirming the highest-priority rung is intact.
- Scenario C (neither per-agent `subagents.model` nor `defaults.subagents.model` set): resolves to the agent's own `model` (`anthropic/claude-opus`) with `source = agent`, confirming the documented last-resort fallback is preserved.

The `node` exit code was `0` (proof script asserts each expectation; first mismatch would throw). The `agent-scope` source labels are produced by the shared `resolveSubagentModelConfigSelectionResult` helper used by both `src/agents/model-selection.ts` and `src/cron/isolated-agent/model-selection.ts`, so a passing scope source label means the cron path inherits the same precedence.

**What was not tested:** Cross-OS runtime (macOS / Windows) — code path is platform-agnostic config resolution, no filesystem or shell dependencies. Live spawn of an actual subagent process against a remote model provider — the resolver returns the same model ref regardless of whether the downstream spawn succeeds, and the spawn path is exercised by `src/agents/openclaw-tools.subagents.sessions-spawn.model.test.ts` (11 passing). UI surfacing of the resolved subagent model in the gateway is also unchanged by this PR and not re-tested here.

target.title: fix(diagnostics-otel): route shared OTLP endpoints per signal
target.body:
Related: #98886

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators enabling multiple diagnostics OTLP signals could send metrics and logs payloads to a traces endpoint when their shared OTLP endpoint already ended in `/v1/traces`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared diagnostics OTLP endpoint fallback now rewrites only a trailing OTLP signal segment to the requested signal path, while explicit traces, metrics, and logs endpoint overrides remain exact per-signal routes. The OpenTelemetry gateway docs now describe that split so shared endpoints and exact signal overrides stay predictable.

## User Impact

Operators can point `diagnostics.otel.endpoint` or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` at a signal-qualified OTLP HTTP URL and enable traces, metrics, and logs without misrouting non-trace payloads. Existing explicit per-signal endpoint overrides keep their current exact behavior.

## Evidence

- Focused proof: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/diagnostics-otel/src/service.test.ts` → 1 file, 97 tests passed (includes the shared-endpoint rewrite and explicit-override exact-route regression tests). Re-run green after the follow-up refactor commit.
- Live OTLP loopback (real-behavior, no mocks): drove the real `@opentelemetry/exporter-*-otlp-proto` v2 exporters (trace/metric/log) against a `127.0.0.1` HTTP receiver with a single shared signal-qualified endpoint `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/api/public/otel/v1/traces?timeout=30s#tenant-a` and all three signals enabled, then recorded the paths each payload actually POSTed to:
  - **Before (old resolver):** metrics and logs both hit `…/v1/traces?timeout=30s` — real misrouting.
  - **After (this PR):** traces→`…/v1/traces`, metrics→`…/v1/metrics`, logs→`…/v1/logs`; the `?timeout=30s` query is preserved on the wire and the `#tenant-a` fragment is dropped (client-side per HTTP spec, never transmitted).
- Whitespace check: `git diff --check` clean.
- Dependency contract: OpenTelemetry Node OTLP/HTTP exporters POST each signal to its own `v1/{traces,metrics,logs}` resource path; a shared endpoint used for multiple signals must be re-pathed per signal, which the loopback above confirms on the wire.
- AI-assisted: yes. Codex implemented the fix; I reviewed, ran a multi-angle code review, folded in a dedup/comment refactor, and produced the live proof above. I understand the code path.
- Proof gaps: loopback receiver is a stub (records paths, returns empty 200); no live vendor backend (Langfuse/Grafana Cloud) run — the routing being verified is client-side URL shaping, which the real exporters exercise identically against any collector.

## Summary

- Why it matters: newly created non-main agents can hit a hard runtime failure even when auth fallback/inheritance is available.
- What changed: when models planning returns `action: "skip"`, `ensureOpenClawModelsJson` now performs a one-time bootstrap from main agent `models.json` only if target is non-main and target `models.json` is missing.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): no continuous global-to-agent sync, no overwrite of existing per-agent `models.json`, no change to `agents.create` behavior itself.

- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

- Root cause: `planOpenClawModelsJson` returns `skip` when providers resolve empty; `ensureOpenClawModelsJson` previously returned early (`wrote: false`) without creating/bootstrapping missing non-main `models.json`.
- Missing detection / guardrail: no fallback path for missing non-main `models.json` in the `skip` branch.
- Prior context (`git blame`, prior PR, issue, or refactor if known): auth store already supports main→non-main inheritance/fallback, but model registry bootstrap was asymmetric.
- Why this regressed now: non-main startup can rely on inherited auth while lacking model catalog file.

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

- Coverage level that should have caught this:
- [x] Unit test

- [ ] End-to-end test
- [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient

```text

-> startup path (providers empty -> skip)
-> no models.json
-> runtime Unknown model

After:
```

target.title: Fix ACP image forwarding and Synology invalid-token throttling
target.body:
## Summary

This PR bundles two small, low-risk fixes:

1. Fix ACP attachment collection so URL-only image attachments are forwarded into ACP turns.
2. Fix Synology Chat invalid-token throttling so the lock engages exactly when the configured budget is exhausted.

## What changed

### ACP image forwarding
Fix ACP attachment collection so image attachments that only provide `MediaUrl` are still forwarded into ACP turns. The dispatcher already uses `MediaAttachmentCache`, which supports both local paths and remote URLs, but URL-only images were skipped before buffer loading. This change removes that path-only gate and adds coverage for remote image attachments while preserving the existing safety behavior that blocked local paths do not fall back to remote URLs.

### Synology invalid-token throttling
Fix the Synology Chat invalid-token rate limiter so a source is locked as soon as it exhausts its configured invalid-token budget. The previous comparison used a strict greater-than check, which allowed one extra invalid attempt before returning 429. This change switches the limiter to threshold-based locking and adds a focused regression test for the exact boundary.

## Validation

- `node scripts/test-projects.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.test.ts extensions/synology-chat/src/webhook-handler.test.ts`

Result on 2026-05-12 after rebasing onto `origin/main` `5abb4b18c8`:

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)  # auto-reply shard
Tests       41 passed (41)

Test Files  1 passed (1)  # extension-messaging shard
Tests       23 passed (23)
```

## Real behavior proof

target.title: feat(irc): support markdown messages via draft/multiline
target.body:
## Summary

Adds support for sending markdown-formatted messages over IRC using the `draft/multiline` CAP extension. This preserves newlines in bot responses, allowing IRC clients to properly render markdown content.

## Motivation

OpenClaw bots typically generate markdown-formatted responses (lists, code blocks, paragraphs). Without multiline support, these get flattened into single lines, making them unreadable on IRC.

The `draft/multiline` spec (https://ircv3.net/specs/extensions/multiline) allows sending multiple lines as a single BATCH, which modern IRC clients can display with proper formatting.

## Changes

- **CAP negotiation**: Requests `draft/multiline` capability on connect, waits for ACK before sending
- **Outgoing BATCH**: Messages with newlines are sent as `BATCH +id draft/multiline #channel` with tagged PRIVMSGs
- **Incoming BATCH**: Multi-line messages received via BATCH are combined into single payload
- **Control chars**: Newlines (`0x0a`) preserved (previously stripped as IRC control chars)
- **Configurable limits**: `textChunkLimit` defaults to 16384 (per spec recommendation)

## Compatibility

- **Servers without draft/multiline**: Falls back to flattening newlines (existing behavior)
- **Clients without draft/multiline**: Will see lines individually (no worse than before)
- **Backwards compatible**: No config changes required

## Testing

Tested on Ergo IRC server with `draft/multiline` support. Bot responses with markdown (lists, code blocks) render correctly in supporting clients.

target.title: Preserve Open WebUI UUID sessions across Control UI
target.body:
## Summary
- preserve Open WebUI UUID chat ids instead of canonicalizing them to `agent:main:<uuid>` in the gateway session store
- normalize `agent:main:<uuid>` back to the original bare UUID when the Control UI reads or writes chat URLs
- pass agent context into transcript lookup so agent-scoped histories resolve the correct transcript file
- add regression coverage for UUID preservation, transcript fallback, and Control UI URL normalization

## Problem
Open WebUI uses opaque UUIDs for chat ids. When the same chat is opened through the OpenClaw Control UI, OpenClaw currently treats that UUID like an ordinary bare session key and canonicalizes it into an agent-prefixed key.

In practice, one Open WebUI conversation can end up with two identities:
- `aa28595d-ef49-4381-b332-e3c990300d74`
- `agent:main:aa28595d-ef49-4381-b332-e3c990300d74`

Once that happens, the Control UI can open an empty shell instead of the real Open WebUI conversation, or it can miss the existing transcript even though the messages are already present on disk.

This is a narrow integration bug rather than a broad session cleanup issue. It shows up when Open WebUI is used as a multi-chat frontend for OpenClaw and the same UUID-backed chat is later opened in the Control UI.

## Why this matters
Open WebUI is a useful ChatGPT-style frontend for OpenClaw because it makes it easy to keep multiple long-running topic-specific chats in the browser. Without this fix, that workflow still requires a downstream monkey patch after upgrades, because the shared Open WebUI/OpenClaw session identity drifts apart.

## What changed
1. Gateway session-key resolution now preserves opaque bare UUIDs instead of rewriting them to agent-scoped keys.
2. The Control UI normalizes `agent:main:<uuid>` URLs back to the original bare UUID and keeps that normalized form in the address bar.
3. Session history loading now carries `agentId` through transcript lookup so agent-scoped stores resolve the right transcript path for these chats.
4. Regression tests cover the gateway store key, transcript fallback, and Control UI URL behavior.

## Scope
This PR intentionally stays focused on shared session identity and transcript lookup for Open WebUI-backed chats.

It does not try to mirror external turns into Open WebUI's own SQLite history database. That visual-sync behavior is a separate follow-up concern.

## Testing
- `pnpm exec vitest run --config vitest.gateway.config.ts src/gateway/session-utils.fs.test.ts -t "uses agentId fallback to read agent-scoped transcripts from OPENCLAW_HOME"`
- `pnpm exec vitest run --config vitest.gateway.config.ts src/gateway/session-utils.test.ts -t "preserves opaque bare UUID session keys"`
- `pnpm exec vitest run --config vitest.unit.config.ts ui/src/ui/app-settings.test.ts`
- manual verification against a deployed Open WebUI + OpenClaw setup on `v2026.3.24`: opening the same UUID-backed chat in the Control UI reused the existing history instead of splitting into a second session

Fixes #49202

target.title: fix(hooks): wire message:sending internal hook to user-defined hooks
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

User-defined `message:sending` hook handlers never fired because no internal bridge existed from the hook runner to outbound message delivery. The hook was defined in the internal hook system but was disconnected from the user-facing hook pipeline.

## Root Cause

The `message:sending` internal hook was emitted via `emitInternalEvent()` in `src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts` but the user-defined hook pipeline (`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`) never subscribed to or forwarded this event.

## Fix

Wire `message:sending` from the internal hook emitter to the user-defined hook pipeline so that hook handlers registered via `[hooks]` configuration receive `message:sending` events before outbound message delivery. Hook handlers can observe, transform, or suppress messages.

## Evidence

### Test Results (vitest 4.1.8)

```
✓ src/hooks/internal-hooks.test.ts (35 tests, 100% pass)

Total: 147 tests, 100% pass
```

All hook and delivery tests pass, covering: message:sending hook wiring to user-defined handlers, hook handler registration, hook lifecycle, outbound delivery with hook integration, heartbeat suppression with message:sending hook, and internal-to-user hook bridge contract.

### Real Behavior Proof

target.title: feat(slack): add ignoreOtherMentions channel config
target.body:
## Summary

- Add `ignoreOtherMentions` option for Slack channel config, mirroring the existing Discord guild/channel feature
- When enabled, messages that mention another user (`<@U...>`) but do not explicitly mention the bot are dropped — even inside bot-participated threads
- This prevents the bot from replying when a user is talking to a coworker in a thread where the bot previously responded

## Slack vs Discord difference

Discord's `ignoreOtherMentions` checks `!wasMentioned && !implicitMention`. The Slack version intentionally omits the `!implicitMention` check because Slack's implicit mention (via `hasSlackThreadParticipation`) fires for **every** message in any bot-participated thread, which would make the feature ineffective.

## Config example

```json5
{
  channels: {
    slack: {
      channels: {
        "*": { ignoreOtherMentions: true },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

## Summary

- Problem: `tools.fs.workspaceOnly` is binary, so operators cannot safely allow agents to read or write a specific host path outside the workspace without opening broader filesystem access.
- Why it matters: multi-tenant and shared-gateway deployments often need narrowly scoped access to shared data, context files, or mounted knowledge directories.
- What changed: added `tools.fs.roots`, an explicit allowlist of filesystem roots with per-root `kind` (`dir`/`file`) and `access` (`ro`/`rw`), wired through host-mode FS tools, `apply_patch`, local media loading, outbound local-media/reply-delivery paths, and prompt-image auto-load.
- Host-mode `read` operations now use pinned file-descriptor root-scoped reads (`readFileWithinRoot`/`openFileWithinRoot`) to close the TOCTOU gap between path validation and file open, in addition to the existing pre-guard.
- Sandbox outbound media delivery now explicitly ignores configured `tools.fs.roots`, preventing sandbox-generated attachments from being rejected when host-mode roots are configured.
- What did NOT change: sandbox mode still relies on Docker isolation and ignores `tools.fs.roots`; `exec` sandboxing is unchanged; `tools.allow` / `tools.deny` behavior is unchanged.

## Change Type (select all)

- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [x] Docs
- [x] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [ ] Auth / tokens

- [x] Integrations
- [x] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- [ ] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Root Cause / Regression History (if applicable)

- Root cause: existing FS policy exposed only two modes for host paths: workspace-only or unrestricted.
- Missing capability: there was no way to express "this agent may read `/data/shared/context.md` but may not read the rest of the host".
- Why now: this is needed for shared-gateway / multi-tenant deployments where the workspace boundary alone is too coarse.
- If unknown, what was ruled out: sandbox mode stays out of scope because sandbox tools resolve container paths, not host paths, and partial host-path enforcement there would create an inconsistent security model.

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

- Coverage level that should catch this:
  - [x] Unit test
  - [x] Seam / integration test
  - [ ] End-to-end test
  - [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient

- Scenarios locked in:
  - lexical dir/file root matching and ro/rw enforcement
  - canonical-root precedence over alias roots for host-mode mutation paths
  - unlink/delete behavior preserving symlink-entry semantics while still respecting stricter canonical roots
  - roots precedence over `workspaceOnly` for host-mode FS access
  - sandbox-mode fallback still honoring `workspaceOnly`
  - rooted local image/PDF/reference-image loads outside the workspace
  - rooted outbound local-media and reply-delivery paths preserving file-vs-dir root semantics
  - rooted prompt-image auto-load outside the workspace
  - host-mode reads use pinned-FD root-scoped operations (TOCTOU-safe)

- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: the risky surfaces here are policy resolution, host-path mutation, and media path propagation, so targeted seam tests catch the actual failure modes without requiring a full live deployment.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- New config surface: `tools.fs.roots` on global `tools.fs` and per-agent `tools.fs`.
- Operators can now grant read-only or read-write access to specific directories/files outside the workspace without granting full host filesystem access.

## Security Impact (required)

### Expected

- Host-mode FS and local media access succeed only within configured roots, respecting `ro` vs `rw`.
- Outbound local-media / reply-delivery flows preserve file-vs-dir root semantics and explicit deny-all behavior.
- Prompt-image auto-load accepts explicitly rooted host paths.
- Sandbox mode ignores `roots` and continues to rely on Docker isolation plus `workspaceOnly` fallback behavior.

### Actual

- Before this change, there was no granular host-path policy between workspace-only and unrestricted host access.

## Evidence

Attach at least one:

- [x] Failing test/log before + passing after

## Human Verification (required)
